summary: Lookout put up in 1910 by the NH Timberland Owners Association; taken down in the late 1970s; the summit is reached by trail in the White Mountain National Forest.

facts.status_note: Tower taken down in the late 1970s; the summit is reached on foot.

staffing.status: Secondary lookout, staffed only in high-risk periods (White Mountain History classification, Osceola named as an example)

access.note: Summit reached by trail in the White Mountain National Forest, from Tripoli Road or the Greeley Pond Trail.

visit.trail_note: A 4.4 km climb from Tripoli Road to the summit, per Friendhike.

events.note: Put up by the NH Timberland Owners Association; NH Family Hikes lists Osceola among the 1910 towers the association paid for.

evidence.supports: Osceola is a 4,340-foot peak in the White Mountains
evidence.quote: Mount Osceola is a 4,340-foot (1,320 m) peak within the White Mountains of New Hampshire

evidence.supports: A fire lookout tower stood at the summit
evidence.quote: There was a fire lookout tower at the top of the mountain

evidence.supports: The Timberland Owners Association built the Osceola lookout
evidence.quote: NHTOA built several lookouts including Sugarloaf, overlooking the Nash Stream watershed, Pine Mountain in Gorham and Osceola near Waterville Valley.

evidence.supports: 1910: ten new towers were constructed that year
evidence.quote: That year, ten new towers were constructed, three of which were on pre-existing hotels or stations.

evidence.supports: Osceola was one of seven towers paid for by the Timberland Owners Association
evidence.quote: The other seven, established on mountains Magalloway, Sugarloaf, Signal, Cambridge Black, Pine, Carrigain, and Osceola, were paid for by the NH Timberland Owners Association.

evidence.supports: Osceola is an example of a secondary lookout: less prominent peak, shorter views, staffed only in high-risk periods
evidence.quote: Secondary Lookouts were on less prominent peaks, with shorter views, and staffed only during high risk periods. Examples are Lonesome Ridge, Osceola and West Royce.

evidence.supports: The tower was taken down in the late 1970s
evidence.quote: but it was taken down in the late 1970s.

evidence.supports: The tower was taken down in the late 1970s (second source)
evidence.quote: Its fire lookout tower was taken down in the late 1970s

evidence.supports: Forest Fire Lookout Association lists the Osceola tower as gone
Summit reached from the Greeley Pond Trail or from Tripoli Road
evidence.quote: Osceola can be ascended from the Greeley Pond Trail to the northeast of the mountain, which requires crossing the East Peak of Osceola first, or from the Tripoli Road to the south.

evidence.supports: The peak lies in the White Mountain National Forest
evidence.quote: Located in the White Mountain National Forest

evidence.supports: Trail from Tripoli Road to the summit is 4.4 km
evidence.quote: A 4.4 km climb on the Mount Osceola Trail from Tripoli Road to the summit of Mount Osceola

evidence.supports: The summit view runs from Mount Washington to Waterville Valley
evidence.quote: the summit view reaches from Mount Washington in the north-east to Waterville Valley in the south

notes_for_editor: Built date 1910 rests on NH Family Hikes and White Mountain History. Removal is only 'late 1970s' in two sources, so no removed event is recorded. Not used: an Upper Pemigewasset Historical Society Facebook post, which could not be fetched (search snippet only), says the lookout ran 1910 to 1958 and was dismantled; a YouTube title describes a 1985 'Mount Osceola fire tower operator' disappearance, which conflicts with the late-1970s removal and is unverified. County check done 2026-10-21: Wikipedia lists Osceola in Grafton County and NH Family Hikes gives the town as Livermore, so the brief's local_unit of Carroll County does not hold; 'Mount Carroll' in the FFLOS row is a unit name, not a county. No source read describes the summit site today.
